lines.text: An illustration: on the first of each month, someone runs a quarterly revenue report on the production database.
It crawls through rows for many minutes.
Meanwhile, checkout gets slow for every customer.
Same data, same SQL — so why does this one query hurt?
lines.say: Same data, same S Q L — so why does this one query hurt?

lines.text: By the end, you'll know where that report belongs, why its database stores data in columns, and how answers computed once come back in seconds.
This video covers the second half of Chapter 3 of Martin Kleppmann's book, Designing Data-Intensive Applications.
lines.say: This video covers the second half of Chapter three of Martin Klepman's book, Designing Data-Intensive Applications.

lines.text: The previous video, Part 1, was about storage engines built for looking things up by key — logs, LSM-trees, and B-trees.
lines.say: The previous video, Part one, was about storage engines built for looking things up by key — logs, L S M trees, and B trees.

lines.text: Our monthly report raises three questions. First: why do analytic queries need their own database?
Second: how should that database lay its data out on disk?
And third: can we avoid computing the same answer over and over?
In our story, checkout is online transaction processing, or OLTP.
lines.say: In our story, checkout is online transaction processing, or O L T P.

lines.text: The report is online analytic processing, or OLAP.
lines.say: The report is online analytic processing, or O L A P.

lines.text: A transaction here just means a quick group of reads and writes — not necessarily full ACID guarantees.
lines.say: A transaction here just means a quick group of reads and writes — not necessarily full acid guarantees.

lines.text: Typically, a transaction reads a few rows by key, while the report aggregates over a huge number of rows.
Transactions write small, random updates as users click; analytics gets its data through bulk imports or event streams.
Transactions serve customers through the app; analytics serves analysts making decisions.
Transactions work on the latest state of things; analytics on the history of everything that happened.
And the sizes typically differ: gigabytes to terabytes, versus terabytes to petabytes.
Put both on one database, and the report starts a huge scan through the tables.
It competes for disk, memory, and CPU with the small transactions customers are waiting on, so those queue up and slow down.
lines.say: It competes for disk, memory, and C P U with the small transactions customers are waiting on, so those queue up and slow down.

lines.text: That's why the people running OLTP databases are reluctant to let analysts run ad hoc, one-off queries on them.
lines.say: That's why the people running O L T P databases are reluctant to let analysts run ad hoc, one-off queries on them.

lines.text: The usual answer is to give analytics a database of its own.
First stop: data warehousing — a separate database, built for answering questions instead of serving customers. So how does our report's data get there?
In a real company, the data behind our report lives in several OLTP systems: orders, payments, a support tool.
lines.say: In a real company, the data behind our report lives in several O L T P systems: orders, payments, a support tool.

lines.text: First, you extract it, with a periodic dump or a continuous stream of changes.
Then you transform it into a schema that's friendly to analysis, and clean it up along the way.
Finally, you load it into the data warehouse — a separate copy that analysts can read but not write.
Extract, transform, load — together, that's called ETL.
lines.say: Extract, transform, load — together, that's called E T L.

lines.text: Now the monthly report can scan as much as it likes without slowing checkout down.
From the outside, a warehouse looks familiar: you still talk to it in SQL, often with the same tools.
lines.say: From the outside, a warehouse looks familiar: you still talk to it in S Q L, often with the same tools.

lines.text: But under the lid, the internals are tuned for a different job — big scans, not quick lookups by key.
As of the book in 2017, commercial warehouses included Teradata, Vertica, SAP HANA, and ParAccel — Amazon Redshift is a hosted version of it.
lines.say: As of the book in twenty seventeen, commercial warehouses included Teradata, Vertica, S A P Hana, and Par Accel — Amazon Redshift is a hosted version of it.

lines.text: And there were open-source SQL-on-Hadoop engines, like Apache Hive, Spark SQL, Cloudera Impala, and Facebook's Presto.
lines.say: And there were open-source S Q L on Hadoop engines, like Apache Hive, Spark S Q L, Cloud-era Impala, and Facebook's Presto.

lines.text: Inside the warehouse, the data usually sits in a star schema, built around one big table in the middle: the fact table.
Each row is one event — here, one payment.
Some columns describe the payment itself, like amount and fee; others are keys pointing into smaller tables.
Those are dimension tables: which merchant, who paid, how they paid, where, and when.
Even the date gets its own dimension, so you can record things like public holidays and filter on them.
Draw the dimensions around the fact table like rays, and you get a star — hence the name.
Real fact tables are wide: often over a hundred columns, sometimes several hundred.
And they get huge: the book describes how a big enterprise may hold tens of petabytes of transaction history, most of it in fact tables.
A variation, the snowflake schema, breaks dimensions into sub-dimensions — a merchant points to its category and its country.
That's more normalized, but stars are often preferred, because they're simpler for analysts to work with.
Keep that width in mind — it's the root of our next problem.
Second stop: column storage. Our report touches a few columns of a very wide table — so how should that table sit on disk?
Here's our report as a query: sum the amount, grouped by country, for last quarter's dates.
Out of a hundred-plus columns, a typical warehouse query like this needs just four or five.
But most databases you know, including the engines from the previous video, store data row by row, with each row's values stored together.
So even with an index on the date, the database loads every matching row from disk, every column of it, and parses it.
Then it throws away almost everything it just read, keeping only the few values the report asked for.
Column storage flips this: each column goes into its own file — here, six files for twelve payments, a simplified illustration.
The trick is that every file keeps the same order, so the fourth entry in each file belongs to payment four.
A mini version of our report — total amount for Germany, DE: the row store reads all 72 cells, the column store only the country and amount files — 24.
lines.say: A mini version of our report — total amount for Germany, D E: the row store reads all seventy-two cells, the column store only the country and amount files — twenty-four.

lines.text: Flip it around and fetch all of payment four: six cells either way, but rows keep them in one place, while columns need six files.
So it's a trade-off: columns win when you scan many rows but few columns; rows win when you need whole records.
Careful: column families in Cassandra and HBase keep a row's values together, so they're mostly row-oriented.
lines.say: Careful: column families in Cassandra and H Base keep a row's values together, so they're mostly row-oriented.

lines.text: Storing by column has a second benefit: values repeat. Here's the country column from our twelve payments.
Only three distinct values across twelve rows.
The book's example is a retailer with billions of sales but only 100,000 distinct products.
lines.say: The book's example is a retailer with billions of sales but only one hundred thousand distinct products.

lines.text: So for each value, keep a bitmap: one bit per row, set to one wherever that row has the value.
Each bitmap is just runs of zeros and ones, so store how long each run is instead, counting zeros first: Germany becomes 0, 3, 6, 2, 1.
lines.say: Each bitmap is just runs of zeros and ones, so store how long each run is instead, counting zeros first: Germany becomes zero, three, six, two, one.

lines.text: That's called run-length encoding.
With many distinct values, like those 100,000 products, each bitmap is mostly zeros, and run-length encoding makes it very compact.
lines.say: With many distinct values, like those one hundred thousand products, each bitmap is mostly zeros, and run-length encoding makes it very compact.

lines.text: Bitmaps can also answer questions directly. Say the report wants Germany or the Netherlands.
Combine those two bitmaps with a bitwise OR, and you have every matching row.
lines.say: Combine those two bitmaps with a bitwise or, and you have every matching row.

lines.text: Conditions on different columns work too: German payments made by card are the Germany bitmap AND the card bitmap — just payment ten.
lines.say: Conditions on different columns work too: German payments made by card are the Germany bitmap and the card bitmap — just payment ten.

lines.text: That only works because every column file keeps the rows in the same order — the same rule that lined up payment four.
Compression pays off twice. When a warehouse scans millions of rows, a big bottleneck is moving data from disk into memory, and from memory into the CPU.
lines.say: Compression pays off twice. When a warehouse scans millions of rows, a big bottleneck is moving data from disk into memory, and from memory into the C P U.

lines.text: A chunk of compressed column holds many rows and fits in the processor's small, fast L1 cache.
lines.say: A chunk of compressed column holds many rows and fits in the processor's small, fast L one cache.

lines.text: The CPU can then run that bitwise AND straight over the compressed chunk, in a tight loop, without calling a function for every value.
lines.say: The C P U can then run that bitwise and straight over the compressed chunk, in a tight loop, without calling a function for every value.

lines.text: The book calls this vectorized processing, and SIMD instructions let one instruction handle many values at once.
lines.say: The book calls this vectorized processing, and sim dee instructions let one instruction handle many values at once.

lines.text: So far, our rows sit in the order they arrived, so the date column jumps around: twelve runs for twelve rows.
You can choose a sort order, but not one column on its own — you'd lose track of which amount belongs to which payment.
Instead, you sort whole rows, even though each column is stored separately — here by date first, then by merchant.
A query for June 2 now reads only that block and skips the rest — just what a last-quarter report wants.
lines.say: A query for June second now reads only that block and skips the rest — just what a last-quarter report wants.

lines.text: Sorting helps compression too: the date column drops from twelve runs to three; merchant, sorted only within each day, has eight; amount stays at twelve.
On billions of rows, the book notes, that first column could shrink to a few kilobytes.
Warehouses keep several copies of the data anyway, so that losing a machine doesn't lose data.
That means each copy can be sorted differently: one by date, one by merchant, one by country.
Each query then uses the copy that fits it best — an idea from a research system called C-Store, adopted by Vertica.
lines.say: Each query then uses the copy that fits it best — an idea from a research system called C Store, adopted by Vertica.

lines.text: Unlike secondary indexes, which only point to rows stored elsewhere, each sort order holds the actual column values.
All this tidiness has a cost, though, when new payments arrive.
Compressed columns can't be updated in place like a B-tree, and a new row that sorts into the middle would most likely mean rewriting every column file.
lines.say: Compressed columns can't be updated in place like a B tree, and a new row that sorts into the middle would most likely mean rewriting every column file.

lines.text: The fix comes from the LSM-trees in the previous video: new writes go into a sorted buffer in memory first.
lines.say: The fix comes from the L S M trees in the previous video: new writes go into a sorted buffer in memory first.

lines.text: When enough have piled up, they're merged with the column files on disk and written out as new files, in bulk.
Queries read both the files and the buffer and combine them, so new data shows up right away — Vertica works this way.
Third stop: precomputed aggregates. The monthly report adds up the same kind of totals every month — can we do that work once and reuse it?
Warehouse queries keep asking for the same aggregates — counts, sums, averages, minimums, maximums — over and over.
A regular, virtual view doesn't help: it's just a saved query that gets expanded and rerun every time you read it.
A materialized view is different: it stores an actual copy of the result on disk, so reading it is cheap.
The catch: whenever the underlying data changes, the view has to be updated too, which makes every write more expensive.
That's why they're not often used in OLTP databases, but in a read-heavy warehouse the trade is often worth it.
lines.say: That's why they're not often used in O L T P databases, but in a read-heavy warehouse the trade is often worth it.

lines.text: A common special case is the data cube: a grid of totals, here revenue by date and merchant, in thousands of dollars, from a larger set of payments.
It's a simplified illustration.
Add up a row and you get one day's total; add up a column and you get one merchant's total — 700 thousand overall.
lines.say: Add up a row and you get one day's total; add up a column and you get one merchant's total — seven hundred thousand overall.

lines.text: Real fact tables have more dimensions, so the grid grows into a cube, and with five dimensions, a five-dimensional hypercube.
Back in our grid, Bolt's revenue across all days is a single lookup: 255 thousand, already computed.
lines.say: Back in our grid, Bolt's revenue across all days is a single lookup: two hundred fifty-five thousand, already computed.

lines.text: But ask about payments over 100 dollars, and the cube can't help, because amount isn't one of its dimensions.
lines.say: But ask about payments over one hundred dollars, and the cube can't help, because amount isn't one of its dimensions.

lines.text: That's why most warehouses keep as much raw data as they can, and treat cubes as a speed-up for common queries.
Let's go back to the first of the month, and that report slowing down checkout.
Checkout got slow because analytics and transactions shared one database; ETL into a warehouse separates them.
lines.say: Checkout got slow because analytics and transactions shared one database; E T L into a warehouse separates them.

lines.text: The report read whole rows; a column store reads only the columns it needs, compressed and sorted by date.
And the same totals, recomputed every month, can come from a materialized view or a cube — an answer in seconds, not many minutes.
Now, some questions for your own system.
Where do your heavy reports run — on the database serving your users, or on a copy built for analysis?
Which of your queries scan millions of rows but use only a few columns?
And which totals do you recompute on every dashboard load that could be computed once?
Next is Chapter 4, Encoding and Evolution: how data written by one version of your code gets read by another.
